0.note: See how you translated the term “chief musician” in the superscription to Psalm 4. Alternate translation: [For the leader of worship music] or [For the music director]

The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **miktam**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.

This superscription is referring to one of two episodes in which David **fled** from King **Saul**, who wanted to kill him, and hid in a **cave**. This could have been the cave of Adullam, as described in 1 Samuel 22:1–2, or the cave of En Gedi, as described in 1 Samuel 24:1–22. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe these events more fully, even though the identity of this cave is not certain. Alternate translation: [David wrote this song while he was hiding in a cave to which he had fled in order to be safe from King Saul]
The superscription is using one part of Saul, his **face**, to mean all of him in his determination to kill David. Alternate translation: [from Saul, who wanted to kill him]

1.note: These are imperatives, but they communicate a polite request rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a polite request. It may be helpful to add an expression such as “please” to make this clear. Alternate translation: [Please be gracious to me; God, please be gracious to me]

David is repeating a phrase in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If speakers of your language can repeat phrases for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [I ask you earnestly to be gracious to me, God]

Here the word **for** does not introduce the reason why God should be gracious to David. It introduces David’s explanation of why he wants God to be gracious to him. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear. It may not be necessary to represent this expression explicitly in your translation.

1.q: בְ⁠ךָ֮ חָסָ֪יָה נַ֫פְשִׁ֥⁠י וּ⁠בְ⁠צֵֽל־כְּנָפֶ֥י⁠ךָ אֶחְסֶ֑ה עַ֝֗ד יַעֲבֹ֥ר הַוּֽוֹת
1.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [my soul takes refuge in the shadow of your wings until the calamities have passed by] or [in you my soul takes refuge, indeed, in the shadow of your wings I take refuge until the calamities have passed by]

David is using one part of himself, his **soul**, to mean all of him in the act of taking refuge in God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in you I take refuge]

David is speaking as if God were actually a **refuge** or place where he could go to be safe. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are the one who keeps me safe]

Here the **shadow** that wings cast represents the area under the wings that they shelter. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and in the shelter of your wings I take refuge] or [and under your wings I take refuge]

David is speaking as if God were actually a bird that had **wings** and as if he were one of that bird’s chicks that would **take refuge** under those wings. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this image as a comparison. The UST models one way to do that.

David is speaking of the **calamities** he is experiencing as if it were living things that could pass by him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [until these calamities end]

2.note: David assumes that his listeners will understand that by **accomplishing**, he means that God accomplishes the purposes that he has for him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the one accomplishing his purposes for me]

3.q: יִשְׁלַ֤ח מִ⁠שָּׁמַ֨יִם ׀ וְֽ⁠יוֹשִׁיעֵ֗⁠נִי חֵרֵ֣ף שֹׁאֲפִ֣⁠י & יִשְׁלַ֥ח אֱ֝לֹהִ֗ים חַסְדּ֥⁠וֹ וַ⁠אֲמִתּֽ⁠וֹ
3.note: The two instances of the verb **send** in this verse are in a form that Hebrew writers could use to express either a statement or a wish. The verb **reproach** would conform to whichever sense the writer intended. At this point in this psalm of supplication, David still seems to be expressing his cry for help, so the ULT translates these verbs as expressing a wish. (See the introduction to this psalm.) However, David may also be making an anticipatory confident statement about what God will do. The original audience may have heard both nuances. Use the verbal form in your language that seems most suitable. Alternate translation: [He will send from the heavens and save me. He will reproach the one trampling me. … God will send his covenant faithfulness and his truth]

David is speaking as if he wanted God actually to **send** someone or something **from the heavens** to **save** him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May he act from the heavens to save me]
If you decide to retain the image of sending in your translation, it may be helpful to specify what God would **send**. Alternate translation: [May he send help from the heavens and save me]

David is speaking as if someone were actually **trampling** on him and as if he wanted God to say something to make the person ashamed of doing that so that he would stop. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May he stop the person who is harassing me]
To translate the term **Selah** here and in verse 7, see how your translation team decided at 3:2 to represent that term.

David is speaking as if **covenant faithfulness** and **truth** were living things that God could **send** to help him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May God act in covenant faithfulness and truth to help me]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **truth** and **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same ideas in other ways, here and in verse 10. Alternate translation: [the ways he is faithful to his covenant and his trustworthiness]

4.note: David is using one part of himself, his **soul** or inner being, to mean all of him in the situation of being **in the midst of lions**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am in the midst of lions]

The word that the ULT translates as **soul** can also mean “life.” The original audience would have heard both nuances. The implication is that David’s life is in danger, that is, he is in danger of being killed. Alternate translation: [My life is in danger because I am in the midst of lions]

David is speaking as if he were actually surrounded by **lions**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this image as a comparison. Alternate translation: [I am in the midst of men who are as dangerous as lions]

By putting the phrase **sons of man** right after **blazing ones**, David is indicating that he is making a comparison between these people and things that are **blazing** and set other things on fire. The point of this comparison is that just as fire is destructive, so these people are trying to destroy him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I must lie down among people who are trying to destroy me]

David is using **sons of man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “human beings.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [human beings]

4.q: שִׁ֭נֵּי⁠הֶם חֲנִ֣ית וְ⁠חִצִּ֑ים וּ֝⁠לְשׁוֹנָ֗⁠ם חֶ֣רֶב חַדָּֽה
4.note: David is using the **teeth** and **tongue** of these men to represent them speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Their speech is a spear and arrows; yes, what they say is a sharp sword]

4.q: שִׁ֭נֵּי⁠הֶם חֲנִ֣ית וְ⁠חִצִּ֑ים וּ֝⁠לְשׁוֹנָ֗⁠ם חֶ֣רֶב חַדָּֽה
4.note: David is speaking as if what these men say with their **teeth** and **tongue** were actually **a spear and arrows** and **a sharp sword**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this image as a comparison. Alternate translation: [What they say about me is as dangerous as a spear or arrows or a sharp sword]

Here the word **tongue** is singular in form, but it refers to the tongues of all of David’s enemies as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “tongue.” Alternate translation: [and their tongues are sharp swords]

5.q: ר֣וּמָ⁠ה עַל־הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֣יִם אֱלֹהִ֑ים עַ֖ל כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ כְּבוֹדֶֽ⁠ךָ
5.note: The expression **Be high** is an imperative, but it communicates a fervent wish rather than a command. Use a form in your language that will indicate this. Alternate translation: [Oh may you be high above the heavens, God, may your glory be above all of the earth]

5.q: ר֣וּמָ⁠ה עַל־הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֣יִם אֱלֹהִ֑ים עַ֖ל כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ כְּבוֹדֶֽ⁠ךָ
5.note: David is speaking as if he actually wanted **God** and his **glory** to be in a physically high position relative to the **heavens** and the **earth**. In this context, God’s **glory** refers to the honor that he receives. The second part of this verse specifies in what way David wants the first part to be true. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [May people honor you, God, more than anyone else in heaven or on earth]

5.q: ר֣וּמָ⁠ה עַל־הַ⁠שָּׁמַ֣יִם אֱלֹהִ֑ים עַ֖ל כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ כְּבוֹדֶֽ⁠ךָ
5.note: David is referring to the entire created realm by naming its two main components, **the heavens** and **the earth**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [May people honor you, God, more than anyone else anywhere]

6.note: The pronoun **They** refers to the enemies whom David describes in verse 4. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [My enemies prepare a net for my steps]

Here, David’s **steps** represent his feet walking along a path. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [They prepare a net for my feet] or [They prepare a net, hoping I will walk into it and it will trap my feet]

David is speaking as if his enemies physically **prepare a net** to trap him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They take measures to capture me]

David is using one part of himself, his **soul** or inner being, to mean all of him in the act of bowing down. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I bow down]

David is speaking as if he physically **bows down** when he realizes that his enemies are trying to capture him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I feel despair]

Here, **to my face** represents “in front of me.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [They dig a pit in front of me; they fall into the midst of it] or [They dig a pit where they expect me to walk, hoping I will fall into it, but they fall into it instead]

David is speaking as if his enemies physically **dig a pit** (covering it to conceal it) in order to trap him, but that they fall into it themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly (indicating that David is elaborating on the idea he expressed in the first part of this verse). Alternate translation: [Indeed, they do things to try to capture me, but what they do only hurts them instead]

7.note: The expression **established** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [My heart is steadfast, God, my heart is steadfast]

David is repeating a phrase in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If speakers of your language can repeat phrases for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [My heart is firmly established, God] or [My heart is firmly steadfast, God]

Here the **heart** represents a person’s feelings and intentions. David means that his confidence in God is unwavering. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have confidence in you, God, I have confidence in you] or [I have resolute confidence in you, God]

David is using a verbal form in which he is addressing himself and suggesting a course of action that is appropriate in light of what he has just said. In your translation, use an appropriate verbal form to indicate this, here and in the next verse. Alternate translation: [So I will sing and make music]

The terms **sing** and **make music** mean similar things. David is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Let me surely sing] or [So I will surely sing]

8.note: David is using the term **glory** to represent his soul. People of this culture spoke of the soul or inner being as the most noble or glorious part of a person. (The use of this term here is similar to its use in 16:9, “my heart rejoices and my glory is glad,” and 30:12, “my glory will make music to you.”) If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Awake, my soul]

David is addressing one part of himself, his **glory** or soul, to tell all of himself to wake up. If your language has a verbal form that is marked for self-address, you could use it here. Other languages may have other ways of showing the meaning. Alternate translation: [I must wake up] or (self-address form) [Wake up!]

David is speaking as if he were actually asleep and needed to wake up. He is actually urging himself to apply vitality and creativity to the work of praising God in song. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [I must sing in a lively way] or (self-address form) [Come on, sing in a lively way]

David is speaking of his **lyre** and **harp** as if they were living things that could wake up from sleep. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will start making music with my lyre and harp]

David is speaking of the **dawn** as if it were a living thing that he could **awaken**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will play them before the sun comes up]

9.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [I will sing praises to you, Lord, among the peoples of other nations]

10.note: Here the word **For** introduces more detailed information about the reasons David has for singing the Lord’s praises. Use a connecting word or phrase in your language that will make this clear. It may not be necessary to represent this word explicitly in your translation. Alternate translation: [I will do this because]

David is speaking of God’s **covenant faithfulness** and **truth** as if they were physical things that could extend from the earth to the **clouds** and the **heavens**. He means that these qualities of God are immeasurably great. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. The UST models one way to do that.

David is using **is great to** as a common expression of his culture to mean “is as high as.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your covenant faithfulness reaches to the heavens] or [your covenant faithfulness is as high as the sky]
See how you translated the abstract nouns for the ideas of **covenant faithfulness** and **truth** in verse 3.

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and your truth is great to the clouds] or [and your truth is as high as the clouds]

11.q: ר֣וּמָ⁠ה עַל־שָׁמַ֣יִם אֱלֹהִ֑ים עַ֖ל כָּל־הָ⁠אָ֣רֶץ כְּבוֹדֶֽ⁠ךָ
11.note: This is the second instance of the refrain in this psalm. We recommend that you show this to your readers by translating the phrases here the same way that you translated them in the first occurrence of this refrain in 57:5.
